Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: Azar was the father of Abraham. He is a name like Israel and Jacob. He was from the people of Kutha, a village in the outskirts of Kufa [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/316.]].

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "He was the father of Abraham."

Sulayman [al-Taymi] said: "It is an insult and a defect. In their speech it means 'the crooked one.'" It was also said that its meaning is "the old man" in Persian, *al-Hanam*. According to these opinions, it is in the genitive position as an apposition (*badal*) or a qualifier (*sifa*), but it is in the accusative form because it is *la yanṣarif* (a diptote, which does not take nunation).

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid and Yaman said: "Azar is the name of an idol." According to this interpretation, it is in the accusative position.

In the speech there is an inversion of order. Its sense is: "Do you take Azar as idols and gods?"

Al-Hasan, Abu Yazid al-Madani and Ya'qub al-Hadrami read *Azaru* with a *damma* (in the vocative), meaning: "O Azar, do you take idols as gods besides God," up to His words ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾.

This means: just as We gave him insight into his religion and the truth in opposition to his people, so We showed him *malakut al-samawat wal-ard*, that is, their dominion. *Al-malakut* means *al-mulk* (sovereignty). The *ta'* in it is added to show intensity, as in *al-jabarut* and *al-rahamut* (the ta' indicates the feminine, or an intensifier, as in these words).

It is reported from the Arabs: "*Sarra'an lahu malakut al-Yaman wal-Iraq*" (a rapid [ruler] whose sovereignty is Yemen and Iraq).

Al-Kisa'i said: "The *ta'* was added to it for emphasis," and he recited:
"And the worst of men is the cheat, the deceiver [*al-khalbut*]" [[Kitab al-'Ayn: 4/271.]].

'Ikrimah said: "It is the sovereignty, except that in Nabataean it is *malkuta*." He read it with a dotted *ya'* as *maliyyan* (meaning sovereignty).

Ibn 'Abbas said: "It means the creation of the heavens and the earth."

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "It means the signs of the heavens and the earth. That is because he was raised up on a rock, and the heavens and the earth were uncovered for him, even the Throne and the lowest part of the earth, and he looked at his place in Paradise."

This is the meaning of His words ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾ [al-'Ankabut 27]: that is, We showed him his place in Paradise.

Qatadah said: Abraham (peace be upon him) said to himself that he was the most merciful of creation. So God, the Mighty and Majestic, raised him until he overlooked the people of the earth and saw their deeds. When he saw them committing acts of disobedience, he said to God: "Destroy them!" and he began to curse them. His Lord said to him: "I am more merciful to My servants than you. Descend, perhaps they will repent."

Qays ibn Abi Hazim narrated from 'Ali, may God honor his face, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When God, the Exalted, showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, he overlooked a man committing one of the sins against God, so he invoked God against him and he perished. Then he overlooked another and invoked God against him and he perished. Then he overlooked another, and when he wanted to invoke against him, God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him: 'O Abraham, you are a man whose supplication is answered. So do not invoke against My servants, for they are in relation to Me in three situations: either they repent to Me and I accept their repentance, or I bring forth from them a soul that glorifies Me, or they [return] to Me. If I wish, I pardon him, and if I wish, I punish him.'"

Al-Dahhak said: "*Malakut al-samawat wal-ard*" is the sun, the moon and the stars. Qatadah said: Abraham (peace be upon him) was hidden from one of the tyrants, and provision was made for him in his fingers: whenever he sucked one of his fingers, he found provision in it. When he came out, God showed him *malakut al-samawat wal-ard*. The *malakut* of the heavens is the sun, the moon and the stars, and the *malakut* of the earth is the mountains, the trees and the seas.

﴿And that he might be among the certain ones.﴾ ﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star...﴾ up to the end of the verse.

The exegetes said: Abraham (peace be upon him) was born in the time of Nimrod ibn Kan'an. Nimrod was the first to place a crown on his head and to put a crown on himself, and he called the people [...]. He had soothsayers and astrologers.

They said: "In this year a boy will be born in your city who will change the religion of the people of the earth, and your destruction and the end of your rule will be at his hands." It is said that they found this in the books of the prophets, peace be upon them.

Al-Suddi said: Nimrod saw in his dream as if a star had risen and taken away the light of the sun and the moon until neither of them had any light. He was terrified by this, a great terror. He summoned the sorcerers, the soothsayers, the magicians and the physiognomists, and asked them about it. They said: "A child will be born in your region this year who will bring about the ruin of your kingdom and your household at his hands."

So he ordered that every boy born in his region that year be slain, and he ordered that men be separated from women, and he appointed a man over every ten [women]. Whenever a woman menstruated, he allowed her to be with him, and when she became pure, he separated her from him. Then Azar, the father of Abraham, returned and found his wife had become pure from menstruation, so he lay with her in her purity, and she conceived Abraham (peace be upon him).

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Nimrod sent to every pregnant woman in his town and detained her with him, except the mother of Abraham, for he did not know of her pregnancy, because she was a young girl who did not recognize pregnancy in her womb.

Al-Suddi said: Nimrod took the men out to the encampment and kept them away from the women, out of fear of that child who might be. He remained in this state as long as God willed. Then he had a need in the city, and he did not trust anyone among his people except Azar, so he sent for him and summoned him. He said: "I have a need of you, and I want to advise you concerning it. I am sending you only because I trust you. I swear to you that you must not approach your wife or lie with her." Azar said: "I am more protective of my religion than that." So he advised him concerning his need, then sent him. He entered the city and fulfilled his need. Then he said: "I entered upon my family and looked at him [the child]." When he looked at the mother of Abraham, he could not restrain himself until he lay with her, and she conceived Abraham.

Ibn 'Abbas said: When the mother of Abraham became pregnant, the soothsayers said to Nimrod: "The boy we told you about has been conceived by his mother tonight." So Nimrod ordered the slaying of the boys. When the mother of Abraham's delivery drew near and her labor pains seized her, she went out fleeing, fearing that someone would see her and kill her child. She placed him in a dry river, then wrapped him in a cloth and placed him among reeds. She returned and reported that she had given birth, and that the child was in such and such a place. Azar went to take him from that place. He dug a tunnel for him beside a river and hid him in it, and sealed its entrance with a rock out of fear of wild beasts. His mother used to visit him and nurse him.

Al-Suddi said: When the belly of the mother of Abraham grew large, Azar feared that [the child] would be slaughtered, so he took her to a land between Kufa and Basra called Urmah. He lodged her in a tunnel in the earth and put water beside them both. He used to visit her secretly, hiding that from his companions. She gave birth in that tunnel, and he grew up. When he was one year old, he was like a three-year-old, and he became a youth, out of fear that [he would fall into] the greed of the slaughterers. Then Azar mentioned to his companions that he had a grown son, and he took him out to them.

Ibn Ishaq said: When the mother of Abraham felt the pains of labor, she went out at night to a cave near her and gave birth to Abraham in it. She tended to his needs as is done for a newborn, then sealed the cave and returned to her house. Then she would look in on him in the cave to see what had happened, and she would find him alive, sucking his thumb.

Abu Rawq said: Whenever the mother of Abraham entered upon Abraham, she found him sucking his fingers. One day she said: "I will look at his fingers." She found him sucking from one finger water, from another honey, from another milk, from another dates, and from another ghee.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Azar had asked the mother of Abraham what had happened with her pregnancy. She said: "I gave birth to a boy, and he died." So he believed her and remained silent about it. A day for Abraham in youth was like a month, and a month like a year. Abraham did not remain in the cave except for fifteen months. Then he returned to his father Azar, and he told him that he was his son, and his mother told him that he was his son, and she informed him of what she had done during his absence. Azar was delighted by that and rejoiced greatly.

They said: Abraham grew up while he was in the tunnel, after he had said to his mother: "Who is my Lord?" She said: "I am." He said: "Then who is your lord?" She said: "Your father." He said: "Then who is the lord of my father?" She said to him: "Be quiet." So he was quiet. When she returned to her husband, she said: "Did you see the boy about whom we used to talk, that he would be of a religion other than that of the people of the earth? He is your son." Then she told him what [Abraham] had said to her. Then his father Azar came to him, and Abraham said to him: "O my father, who is my Lord?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who is my mother's lord?" He said: "I am." He said: "Then who is your lord?" He said: "Nimrod." He said: "Then who is the lord of Nimrod?" So [Azar] slapped him a slap and said: "Be quiet and get up!" He said to his parents: "Take me out." So they took him out of the tunnel. They set out with him when the sun had set. Abraham looked at the camels, the horses and the sheep, and said: "Father, what are these?" He said: "Camels, horses and sheep." He said: "These must have a lord and a creator." Then he looked and reflected on the creation of the heavens and the earth. He said: "The One who created me, provided for me, fed me and gave me drink, He is my Lord; I have no god besides Him." Then he looked, and behold, Jupiter had risen, and it is said Venus; that night was at the end of the month, so he saw the star before the moon. He said: ﴿This is my lord.﴾

That is His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾, that is, it entered. It is said: *janna al-layl* and *ajanna*, and *janahu al-layl* and *ajannahu*, and *janna 'alayhi al-layl yajunnu junuunan wa jinanan* when it grew dark and everything passed away. The jinn are so called because they are hidden [*ijtinan*], so they are not seen.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *junun al-layl* is its blackness. He recited:
"Had it not been for the darkness of night, the pursuit of our riders would have overtaken him, at Dhu al-Ramth and al-Arta, 'Iyad ibn Nashib" [[al-Sihah: 5/2094, where it reads "rikabuna" (our riders); Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/25. *Al-Ramth* with a kasra is the pasture of camels, and *al-Arta* is a tree that grows in sand.]].

﴿And he saw a star, [and] said, "This is my lord."﴾ They differed concerning it. Some of them took it according to its apparent meaning and said: Abraham (peace be upon him) was not one who sought guidance, bewildered, seeking success, until God granted him success and gave him his rectitude. This statement of his was made in his childhood, before the proof was established against him. In that condition one would say that neither disbelief nor faith exists.

Evidence for this is what 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "When ﴿the night covered him, he saw a star, [and] said, 'This is my lord.'﴾ He worshipped it until it set. When it set, he said, ﴿'I do not like those that set.'﴾ When he saw the moon rising, he said, ﴿'This is my lord,'﴾ and worshipped it until it set. When it set, ﴿'If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray.'﴾ When he saw the sun rising, he said, ﴿'This is my lord; this is greater,'﴾ and worshipped it until the sun set. When it set, he said: ﴿'O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate.'﴾"

Others rejected this view and said: It is not permissible that a messenger of God should come upon a time when he was not monotheistic, knowing, and free from every worshipped other than Him.

They said: How could they accuse him of this, when God protected and purified him in his place of rest and his place of storage, and granted him his rectitude beforehand, and showed him His dominion, and He said: ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat 84], and He said: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am 75]? "He saw a star and said, 'This is my lord,'" based on belief and reality? This is something that could never happen.

Then four interpretations were given of it. The first interpretation: Abraham (peace be upon him) wanted to lead them step by step with this statement, to make them recognize their error and ignorance in exalting what they exalted, and to establish the proof against them, and to show them that he exalted what they exalted, and sought guidance from where they sought it. When [the star] set, he showed them the deficiency inherent in the stars, so they would see the error of what they claimed. They used to exalt the stars, worship them, and treat them as judges.

They said: The likeness of this is like the disciple (*al-hawari*) who came to a people who worshipped their idol, and he showed them its greatness, and they were guided by his opinion in many matters, until an enemy of theirs, whom the king feared for his kingdom, reproached them, and the king consulted the disciple about his affair.

They said [to the disciple]: "Our opinion is that you should call upon our god so that what has misled us may be removed, for we are gathered for such a day." So they gathered around it, crying out and supplicating, while their enemy hurried and relied [on that]. When it became clear to them that their lord neither benefits nor harms, he said to them, in the form of a question and a reproach for their action: ﴿This is my lord?﴾ And could such a thing be a lord? That is, this is not my lord, like God's words ﴿'Or you will be among the immortals'﴾ [al-A'raf 20], meaning that they are the immortals.

And like Moses' words to Pharaoh: ﴿And is it a favor of which you remind me that you have enslaved the children of Israel?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 22], meaning: "Or is it a favor that you have granted?"

Al-Hudhali said:
"They raised me up and said, 'O Khuwaylid, do not be alarmed,'
so I said, and I denied the faces, 'They, they [are the ones]'" [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/325; al-Sihah: 3/1223; the verse is by Abu Khirash.]].

Another said:
"By your life, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable,
whether [he is] Shu'ayth ibn Sahm or Shu'ayth ibn Munqir" [[Same source.]].

The third interpretation: Abraham (peace be upon him) said this as an argument against his people, not in the sense of doubt about his Lord, as if he said: "This is my lord according to you." ﴿When it set, he said—and it was the crescent—﴾ he said: "This is greater than it," so he looked at what you were devoted to here, meaning with you. His words ﴿'Taste! Indeed you are the mighty, the noble'﴾ [al-Dukhan 49], with his saying to Abu Jahl [the trial in the fire]: "You are such in your own estimation, but in our view you are neither mighty nor noble." There is abbreviation and implication in the verse, and its meaning is: he said, "They say, 'This is my lord,'" like His words ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael [said], "Our Lord..."﴾ [al-Baqarah 127], meaning they say: "Our Lord, accept from us." ﴿When it set, that is, disappeared and vanished, he said: "I do not like those that set"﴾ as lords, for they do not last. ﴿When he saw the moon rising, that is, ascending, he said, "This is my lord." When it set, he said, "If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray,"﴾ from guidance. ﴿When he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord."﴾

Muhammad ibn Muqatil al-Razi said: He said "This" [masculine] and not "This" [feminine] because he saw the light of the sun and did not see the sun itself, so he returned it to the ray.

Al-Akhfash said: He meant: "This one who rises is my lord," or "This one who comes, I see him as my lord." "This is greater," because he saw it as brighter and greater. When it set, he said: ﴿"O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate. Indeed I have turned my face toward..."﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Azar used to make idols. When Abraham was taken into his care, he began to make idols and give them to Abraham to sell. Abraham would take them and call out: "Who will buy what harms him and does not benefit him?" No one would buy them. When they became too many for him, he took them to a river, struck their heads in it, and said: "Drink!" mocking his people and the error they were in, until his disparagement of them and his mockery of them became widespread among his people and the people of his town.

﴿And his people disputed with him,﴾ that is, argued with him about his religion. ﴿He said, "Do you argue with me about God, when He has guided me?"﴾ that is, He informed me of monotheism and the truth. ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾. That is because they said to him: "Are you not afraid that our gods will afflict you with harm, such as leprosy or madness, because of your disparagement of them?" He said to them: ﴿"And I do not fear what you associate with Him," that is, the idols, "except that my Lord wills something." Everything is in accordance with what He wills, ﴿"My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge"﴾, that is, His knowledge encompasses everything. ﴿"Will you not then remember? And how should I fear what you have associated, when you do not fear that you have associated with God that for which He has sent down no authority to you?"﴾ That is, the idols, which do not see, do not hear, do not harm and do not benefit. ﴿"Then which of the two parties has more right to security, if you know?"﴾ That is, more worthy of security [are we, or whoever follows my religion?]. Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, said, judging and deciding between them: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing [zulm]—for them is security, and they are guided.﴾ That is, they did not mix their faith with shirk: ﴿for them is security, and they are guided﴾.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: When this verse was revealed, the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) took it to apply to themselves and said: "We have not wronged ourselves." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is not as you think; rather, it is as Luqman said to his son: ﴿'O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association is a great wrong'﴾ [Luqman 13]" [142] (It is only shirk).

﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people﴾, that is, to overcome their argument and defeat them with proof. He said: it is His words ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾; he said: "with worship of idols." ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, by knowledge.

The people of Kufa, Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Mahisin read *darajatin* with tanwin, meaning: "We raise whom We will by degrees." Its like is in Surah Yusuf: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾.

And when Abraham said to his father Azar, ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾

Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: Azar was the father of Abraham. He is a name like Israel and Jacob. He was from the people of Kutha, a village in the outskirts of Kufa [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/316.]].

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "He was the father of Abraham."

Then he returned to his father Azar, and he told him that he was his son, and his mother told him that he was his son, and she informed him of what she had done during his absence. Azar was delighted by that and rejoiced greatly.

They said: Abraham grew up while he was in the tunnel, after he had said to his mother: "Who is my Lord?" She said: "I am." He said: "Then who is your lord?" She said: "Your father." He said: "Then who is the lord of my father?" She said to him: "Be quiet." So he was quiet. When she returned to her husband, she said: "Did you see the boy about whom we used to talk, that he would be of a religion other than that of the people of the earth? He is your son." Then she told him what [Abraham] had said to her. Then his father Azar came to him, and Abraham said to him: "O my father, who is my Lord?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who is my mother's lord?" He said: "I am." He said: "Then who is your lord?" He said: "Nimrod." He said: "Then who is the lord of Nimrod?" So [Azar] slapped him a slap and said: "Be quiet and get up!" He said to his parents: "Take me out." So they took him out of the tunnel. They set out with him when the sun had set. Abraham looked at the camels, the horses and the sheep, and said: "Father, what are these?" He said: "Camels, horses and sheep." He said: "These must have a lord and a creator." Then he looked and reflected on the creation of the heavens and the earth. He said: "The One who created me, provided for me, fed me and gave me drink, He is my Lord; I have no god besides Him." Then he looked, and behold, Jupiter had risen, and it is said Venus; that night was at the end of the month, so he saw the star before the moon. He said: ﴿This is my lord.﴾

That is His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾, that is, it entered. It is said: *janna al-layl* and *ajanna*, and *janahu al-layl* and *ajannahu*, and *janna 'alayhi al-layl yajunnu junuunan wa jinanan* when it grew dark and everything passed away. The jinn are so called because they are hidden [*ijtinan*], so they are not seen.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *junun al-layl* is its blackness. He recited:
"Had it not been for the darkness of night, the pursuit of our riders would have overtaken him, at Dhu al-Ramth and al-Arta, 'Iyad ibn Nashib" [[al-Sihah: 5/2094, where it reads "rikabuna" (our riders); Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/25. *Al-Ramth* with a kasra is the pasture of camels, and *al-Arta* is a tree that grows in sand.]].

﴿And he saw a star, [and] said, "This is my lord."﴾ They differed concerning it. Some of them took it according to its apparent meaning and said: Abraham (peace be upon him) was not one who sought guidance, bewildered, seeking success, until God granted him success and gave him his rectitude. This statement of his was made in his childhood, before the proof was established against him. In that condition one would say that neither disbelief nor faith exists.

Evidence for this is what 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "When ﴿the night covered him, he saw a star, [and] said, 'This is my lord.'﴾ He worshipped it until it set. When it set, he said, ﴿'I do not like those that set.'﴾ When he saw the moon rising, he said, ﴿'This is my lord,'﴾ and worshipped it until it set. When it set, ﴿'If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray.'﴾ When he saw the sun rising, he said, ﴿'This is my lord; this is greater,'﴾ and worshipped it until the sun set. When it set, he said: ﴿'O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate.'﴾"

Others rejected this view and said: It is not permissible that a messenger of God should come upon a time when he was not monotheistic, knowing, and free from every worshipped other than Him.

They said: How could they accuse him of this, when God protected and purified him in his place of rest and his place of storage, and granted him his rectitude beforehand, and showed him His dominion, and He said: ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat 84], and He said: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am 75]? "He saw a star and said, 'This is my lord,'" based on belief and reality? This is something that could never happen.

Then four interpretations were given of it. The first interpretation: Abraham (peace be upon him) wanted to lead them step by step with this statement, to make them recognize their error and ignorance in exalting what they exalted, and to establish the proof against them, and to show them that he exalted what they exalted, and sought guidance from where they sought it. When [the star] set, he showed them the deficiency inherent in the stars, so they would see the error of what they claimed. They used to exalt the stars, worship them, and treat them as judges.

They said: The likeness of this is like the disciple (*al-hawari*) who came to a people who worshipped their idol, and he showed them its greatness, and they were guided by his opinion in many matters, until an enemy of theirs, whom the king feared for his kingdom, reproached them, and the king consulted the disciple about his affair.

They said [to the disciple]: "Our opinion is that you should call upon our god so that what has misled us may be removed, for we are gathered for such a day." So they gathered around it, crying out and supplicating, while their enemy hurried and relied [on that]. When it became clear to them that their lord neither benefits nor harms, he said to them, in the form of a question and a reproach for their action: ﴿This is my lord?﴾ And could such a thing be a lord? That is, this is not my lord, like God's words ﴿'Or you will be among the immortals'﴾ [al-A'raf 20], meaning that they are the immortals.

And like Moses' words to Pharaoh: ﴿And is it a favor of which you remind me that you have enslaved the children of Israel?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 22], meaning: "Or is it a favor that you have granted?"

Al-Hudhali said:
"They raised me up and said, 'O Khuwaylid, do not be alarmed,'
so I said, and I denied the faces, 'They, they [are the ones]'" [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/325; al-Sihah: 3/1223; the verse is by Abu Khirash.]].

Another said:
"By your life, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable,
whether [he is] Shu'ayth ibn Sahm or Shu'ayth ibn Munqir" [[Same source.]].

The third interpretation: Abraham (peace be upon him) said this as an argument against his people, not in the sense of doubt about his Lord, as if he said: "This is my lord according to you." ﴿When it set, he said—and it was the crescent—﴾ he said: "This is greater than it," so he looked at what you were devoted to here, meaning with you. His words ﴿'Taste! Indeed you are the mighty, the noble'﴾ [al-Dukhan 49], with his saying to Abu Jahl [the trial in the fire]: "You are such in your own estimation, but in our view you are neither mighty nor noble." There is abbreviation and implication in the verse, and its meaning is: he said, "They say, 'This is my lord,'" like His words ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael [said], "Our Lord..."﴾ [al-Baqarah 127], meaning they say: "Our Lord, accept from us." ﴿When it set, that is, disappeared and vanished, he said: "I do not like those that set"﴾ as lords, for they do not last. ﴿When he saw the moon rising, that is, ascending, he said, "This is my lord." When it set, he said, "If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray,"﴾ from guidance. ﴿When he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord."﴾

Muhammad ibn Muqatil al-Razi said: He said "This" [masculine] and not "This" [feminine] because he saw the light of the sun and did not see the sun itself, so he returned it to the ray.

Al-Akhfash said: He meant: "This one who rises is my lord," or "This one who comes, I see him as my lord." "This is greater," because he saw it as brighter and greater. When it set, he said: ﴿"O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate. Indeed I have turned my face toward..."﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Azar used to make idols. When Abraham was taken into his care, he began to make idols and give them to Abraham to sell. Abraham would take them and call out: "Who will buy what harms him and does not benefit him?" No one would buy them. When they became too many for him, he took them to a river, struck their heads in it, and said: "Drink!" mocking his people and the error they were in, until his disparagement of them and his mockery of them became widespread among his people and the people of his town.

﴿And his people disputed with him,﴾ that is, argued with him about his religion. ﴿He said, "Do you argue with me about God, when He has guided me?"﴾ that is, He informed me of monotheism and the truth. ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾. That is because they said to him: "Are you not afraid that our gods will afflict you with harm, such as leprosy or madness, because of your disparagement of them?" He said to them: ﴿"And I do not fear what you associate with Him," that is, the idols, "except that my Lord wills something." Everything is in accordance with what He wills, ﴿"My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge"﴾, that is, His knowledge encompasses everything. ﴿"Will you not then remember? And how should I fear what you have associated, when you do not fear that you have associated with God that for which He has sent down no authority to you?"﴾ That is, the idols, which do not see, do not hear, do not harm and do not benefit. ﴿"Then which of the two parties has more right to security, if you know?"﴾ That is, more worthy of security [are we, or whoever follows my religion?]. Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, said, judging and deciding between them: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing [zulm]—for them is security, and they are guided.﴾ That is, they did not mix their faith with shirk: ﴿for them is security, and they are guided﴾.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: When this verse was revealed, the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) took it to apply to themselves and said: "We have not wronged ourselves." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is not as you think; rather, it is as Luqman said to his son: ﴿'O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association is a great wrong'﴾ [Luqman 13]" [142] (It is only shirk).

﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people﴾, that is, to overcome their argument and defeat them with proof. He said: it is His words ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾; he said: "with worship of idols." ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, by knowledge.

The people of Kufa, Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Mahisin read *darajatin* with tanwin, meaning: "We raise whom We will by degrees." Its like is in Surah Yusuf: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾.

God ﷻ says: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob; each We guided﴾, meaning We set them on the right path and directed them, ﴿and Noah We guided before, and of his offspring﴾, meaning Abraham's descendants, and among them David and Solomon, meaning his son. The phrase "and of his offspring" also means, according to this reading, David and Noah, because David was not a descendant of Abraham. He is David ibn Ayshā. ﴿And Job﴾, who is Job ibn [Amūṣ ibn Rānzakh ibn] [[Thus in the original.]] Rūḥ ibn ʿĪṣā ibn Isaac ibn Abraham. ﴿And Joseph﴾, who is Joseph ibn Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham. Concerning him the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the noble one, son of the noble one, son of the noble one, is Joseph ibn Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham." [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 4/356.]] [143]

﴿And Moses﴾, who is Moses ibn ʿImrān ibn [Ṣahr ibn Fāʿith ibn Lād] [[Thus in the original.]] ibn Jacob.

﴿And Aaron﴾, who is the brother of Moses, older than him by one year. ﴿Thus﴾, meaning as We rewarded Abraham for his monotheism and his steadfastness in his religion, by raising his rank and granting him prophet-children who were pious, ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾ for their goodness. ﴿And Zachariah﴾, who is Zachariah ibn Azan ibn Barkiyā. [[Tafsir al-Ṭabarī: 7/340.]] ﴿And John﴾, who is his son. ﴿And Jesus﴾, who is the son of Mary, daughter of ʿImrān ibn Ashīm ibn Amūn ibn Ḥizqiyā. ﴿And Elias﴾.

They differed concerning him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: he is Idrīs, like Jacob and Israel.

Others said: he is Elias ibn Bastī ibn Fankhāṣ ibn al-ʿAyzār ibn Aaron ibn ʿImrān, the Prophet of God (peace be upon him). And he is [al-Naṣīḥ], because God Most High attributed in this verse the people to Noah and made them his offspring, and Noah is the son of Lamech ibn Methuselah ibn Enoch, who is Idrīs. It is impossible that the grandfather of his father be described as being from his offspring. [[Tafsir al-Ṭabarī: 7/340.]] ﴿And each of the righteous﴾, meaning the prophets and the believers. ﴿And Ishmael﴾, who is the son of Abraham. ﴿And Elisha﴾, who is Elisha ibn Akhṭūb ibn al-ʿAjūn. ﴿And Jonah﴾, who is Jonah ibn Matta. ﴿And Lot﴾, who is Lot ibn Aaron, or the son of the brother of Abraham (peace be upon him). ﴿And each We preferred over the worlds﴾, meaning the worlds of their own times. ﴿And from their fathers, their offspring and their brothers﴾, ﴿and We chose them﴾, meaning We tested them and selected them, ﴿and We guided them﴾, meaning We made them firm and directed them, ﴿to a straight path. That is the guidance of God; He guides whom He wills of His servants. And if they had associated﴾, meaning if these prophets whom we have named had associated others with their Lord, Exalted is His remembrance, and worshipped someone besides Him, ﴿then would have failed from them﴾, meaning would have been nullified and gone from them, ﴿what they used to do. Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book﴾, meaning those scriptures, ﴿and the judgment and the prophethood. So if these disbelieve in them﴾, meaning the Quraysh, ﴿then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾, meaning the Helpers (al-Anṣār) and the people of Medina.

Qatāda said: it means the eighteen prophets whom God the Mighty and Majestic mentioned: ﴿Those are the ones whom God has guided, so follow their guidance﴾, meaning follow their practice and their way. In "iqtadih" the hā' is the hā' of pause (hā' al-waqf). ﴿Say: I ask of you no reward for it﴾, meaning no wage or provision. ﴿It is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) is not but an admonition to the worlds. ﴿And they did not measure God with His true measure﴾, meaning they did not magnify God with His true magnificence, and did not describe God with His true description, ﴿when they said: God has not sent down anything upon a human being﴾.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: a man from the Jews of the Anṣār, called Mālik ibn al-Ṣayf, came disputing with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet said: "Do you associate partners with God, who sent down the Torah to Moses? Do you not find in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?" He was a fat rabbi (ḥabr, a Jewish scholar), so he became angry and said: "God has not sent down anything upon a human being." He said to his companions who were with him: "Woe to you! Nor Moses?" He said: "[By God], God has not sent down anything upon a human being." Then God the Mighty and Majestic revealed this verse.

Al-Suddī said: it was revealed concerning Fanḥāṣ ibn ʿAzūrā, who was the one who said this statement.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī: some Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was sitting with his knees raised, and they said: "O Abū al-Qāsim, will you not bring us a book from heaven, as Moses (peace be upon him) brought tablets carried from God?"

So God the Mighty and Majestic revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven. They had asked Moses for greater than that﴾ [[Tafsir al-Ṭabarī: 7/348; Asbāb al-Nuzūl of al-Wāḥidī: 143.]], the verse.

Then a man from the Jews came and said: "God has not sent down anything upon you, nor upon Moses, nor upon Jesus, nor upon anyone." So God revealed this verse.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: the Jews said: "O Muḥammad, has God sent down a book upon you?" He said: "Yes." They said: "By God, God has not sent down from heaven any book." So God revealed ﴿And they did not measure God with His true measure﴾ [[Sūrat al-Anʿām: 91.]].

Muʿallā ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, from Ibn ʿAbbās: it was revealed concerning the disbelievers who denied God's power over them. Whoever affirms that God is over all things capable has measured God with His true measure, and whoever does not believe in that has not measured God with His true measure.

Mujāhid said: it was revealed concerning a man from the Quraysh. They said: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human being.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought…﴾ up to His saying ﴿and you conceal much﴾, he said: they are the Jews.

As for His saying: ﴿and you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾, he said: this is addressed to the Muslims, and so on.

Ayyūb narrated from him that he recited ﴿and you were taught﴾ addressing the Arabs: ﴿what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾.

As for His saying ﴿You make it into qarāṭīs﴾, meaning scrolls (dafātir), the plural of qirṭās, meaning you separate them and write them in separate scrolls, so that they are not gathered together, in order to hide from them what you wish, and so that the common people do not notice them. ﴿You disclose them and conceal much﴾, of the mention of Muḥammad, the verse of stoning, and similar things that they wrote down.

Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlā recited: يجعلونه قراطيس يبدونها ويخفون كثيرا, all with the ya', as a report about them.

The rest recited them with the ta', as address, and their proof is what precedes it of address: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book…﴾.

And after it He says: ﴿and you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾. So if they answer you and say: ﴿…﴾ and otherwise, then ﴿Say: God﴾ did that. ﴿Then leave them in their discourse, playing﴾: this is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) and not an answer; its implied meaning is "leave them in their discourse, playing," i.e., ﴿leave them in their discourse, playing﴾ as a participle.

God ﷻ says: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob; each We guided﴾, meaning We set them on the right path and directed them, ﴿and Noah We guided before, and of his offspring﴾, meaning Abraham's descendants, and among them David and Solomon, meaning his son. The phrase "and of his offspring" also means, according to this reading, David and Noah, because David was not a descendant of Abraham. He is David ibn Ayshā. ﴿And Job﴾, who is Job ibn [Amūṣ ibn Rānzakh ibn] [[Thus in the original.]] Rūḥ ibn ʿĪṣā ibn Isaac ibn Abraham. ﴿And Joseph﴾, who is Joseph ibn Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham. Concerning him the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the noble one, son of the noble one, son of the noble one, is Joseph ibn Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham." [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 4/356.]] [143]

﴿And Moses﴾, who is Moses ibn ʿImrān ibn [Ṣahr ibn Fāʿith ibn Lād] [[Thus in the original.]] ibn Jacob.

﴿And Aaron﴾, who is the brother of Moses, older than him by one year. ﴿Thus﴾, meaning as We rewarded Abraham for his monotheism and his steadfastness in his religion, by raising his rank and granting him prophet-children who were pious, ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾ for their goodness. ﴿And Zachariah﴾, who is Zachariah ibn Azan ibn Barkiyā. [[Tafsir al-Ṭabarī: 7/340.]] ﴿And John﴾, who is his son. ﴿And Jesus﴾, who is the son of Mary, daughter of ʿImrān ibn Ashīm ibn Amūn ibn Ḥizqiyā. ﴿And Elias﴾.

They differed concerning him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: he is Idrīs, like Jacob and Israel.

Others said: he is Elias ibn Bastī ibn Fankhāṣ ibn al-ʿAyzār ibn Aaron ibn ʿImrān, the Prophet of God (peace be upon him). And he is [al-Naṣīḥ], because God Most High attributed in this verse the people to Noah and made them his offspring, and Noah is the son of Lamech ibn Methuselah ibn Enoch, who is Idrīs. It is impossible that the grandfather of his father be described as being from his offspring. [[Tafsir al-Ṭabarī: 7/340.]] ﴿And each of the righteous﴾, meaning the prophets and the believers. ﴿And Ishmael﴾, who is the son of Abraham. ﴿And Elisha﴾, who is Elisha ibn Akhṭūb ibn al-ʿAjūn. ﴿And Jonah﴾, who is Jonah ibn Matta. ﴿And Lot﴾, who is Lot ibn Aaron, or the son of the brother of Abraham (peace be upon him). ﴿And each We preferred over the worlds﴾, meaning the worlds of their own times. ﴿And from their fathers, their offspring and their brothers﴾, ﴿and We chose them﴾, meaning We tested them and selected them, ﴿and We guided them﴾, meaning We made them firm and directed them, ﴿to a straight path. That is the guidance of God; He guides whom He wills of His servants. And if they had associated﴾, meaning if these prophets whom we have named had associated others with their Lord, Exalted is His remembrance, and worshipped someone besides Him, ﴿then would have failed from them﴾, meaning would have been nullified and gone from them, ﴿what they used to do. Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book﴾, meaning those scriptures, ﴿and the judgment and the prophethood. So if these disbelieve in them﴾, meaning the Quraysh, ﴿then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾, meaning the Helpers (al-Anṣār) and the people of Medina.

Qatāda said: it means the eighteen prophets whom God the Mighty and Majestic mentioned: ﴿Those are the ones whom God has guided, so follow their guidance﴾, meaning follow their practice and their way. In "iqtadih" the hā' is the hā' of pause (hā' al-waqf). ﴿Say: I ask of you no reward for it﴾, meaning no wage or provision. ﴿It is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) is not but an admonition to the worlds. ﴿And they did not measure God with His true measure﴾, meaning they did not magnify God with His true magnificence, and did not describe God with His true description, ﴿when they said: God has not sent down anything upon a human being﴾.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: a man from the Jews of the Anṣār, called Mālik ibn al-Ṣayf, came disputing with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet said: "Do you associate partners with God, who sent down the Torah to Moses? Do you not find in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?" He was a fat rabbi (ḥabr, a Jewish scholar), so he became angry and said: "God has not sent down anything upon a human being." He said to his companions who were with him: "Woe to you! Nor Moses?" He said: "[By God], God has not sent down anything upon a human being." Then God the Mighty and Majestic revealed this verse.

Al-Suddī said: it was revealed concerning Fanḥāṣ ibn ʿAzūrā, who was the one who said this statement.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī: some Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was sitting with his knees raised, and they said: "O Abū al-Qāsim, will you not bring us a book from heaven, as Moses (peace be upon him) brought tablets carried from God?"

So God the Mighty and Majestic revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven. They had asked Moses for greater than that﴾ [[Tafsir al-Ṭabarī: 7/348; Asbāb al-Nuzūl of al-Wāḥidī: 143.]], the verse.

Then a man from the Jews came and said: "God has not sent down anything upon you, nor upon Moses, nor upon Jesus, nor upon anyone." So God revealed this verse.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: the Jews said: "O Muḥammad, has God sent down a book upon you?" He said: "Yes." They said: "By God, God has not sent down from heaven any book." So God revealed ﴿And they did not measure God with His true measure﴾ [[Sūrat al-Anʿām: 91.]].

Mujāhid said: it was revealed concerning a man from the Quraysh. They said: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human being.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought…﴾ up to His saying ﴿and you conceal much﴾, he said: they are the Jews.

As for His saying: ﴿and you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾, he said: this is addressed to the Muslims, and so on.

Ayyūb narrated from him that he recited ﴿and you were taught﴾ addressing the Arabs: ﴿what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾.

As for His saying ﴿You make it into qarāṭīs﴾, meaning scrolls (dafātir), the plural of qirṭās, meaning you separate them and write them in separate scrolls, so that they are not gathered together, in order to hide from them what you wish, and so that the common people do not notice them. ﴿You disclose them and conceal much﴾, of the mention of Muḥammad, the verse of stoning, and similar things that they wrote down.

The rest recited them with the ta', as address, and their proof is what precedes it of address: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book…﴾.

And after it He says: ﴿and you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾. So if they answer you and say: ﴿…﴾ and otherwise, then ﴿Say: God﴾ did that. ﴿Then leave them in their discourse, playing﴾: this is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) and not an answer; its implied meaning is "leave them in their discourse, playing," i.e., ﴿leave them in their discourse, playing﴾ as a participle.

God ﷻ says: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob; each We guided﴾, meaning We set them on the right path and directed them, ﴿and Noah We guided before, and of his offspring﴾, meaning Abraham's descendants, and among them David and Solomon, meaning his son. Wait—I need to translate the passage faithfully as it stands, so here is the full translation:

This is a Book (yaʿnī al-Qur'ān, i.e., the Qur'an) which We have sent down, blessed (mubārak), meaning: and this is a blessed Book which We have sent down, confirming (muṣaddiq) that which is before it (alladhī bayna yadayhi), and that you may warn (wa-li-tundhira)... [text informs]: This is the report.

And Ibn ʿĀmir—no. Ṣ: Ā‘ṣim recited: with the yāʾ, i.e., "and that He may warn" (wa-liyundhira) the Book.

The Mother of the Cities (ʾUmm al-Qurā): that is Mecca; it was named the Mother of the Cities because the earth was spread out from beneath it (duḥiyat), and "those around it" (wa-man ḥawlahā): the whole earth is carried, east and west.

Those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, that is, in the Book, and they guard their prayers (ʿalā ṣalātihim yuḥāfiẓūn): meaning the five prayers; they persevere in them.

And who is more unjust (man aẓlamu) — i.e., more mistaken in speech and more ignorant in deed — than one who fabricates (iftarā) against God a lie (kadhiban), claiming that He has sent him as a prophet, and says: "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him?

It was revealed concerning Musaylima al-Kadhdhāb al-Ḥanafī, who used to eavesdrop, practise soothsaying, claim prophethood, and assert that God had revealed to him. He had sent two men to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Do you testify that Musaylima is a prophet?" They said: "Yes." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Were it not that messengers are not killed, I would have struck off your necks."

[Musnad Aḥmad: 3/488.]

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw in a dream that in my hands were two gold bracelets (shawārīn), and they weighed heavily on me and troubled me. God revealed to me that I should blow on them, so I blew, and they flew away. I interpreted them as the two liars between whom I am: the liar of Yamāma, Musaylima, and the liar of Ṣanʿāʾ, al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī."

[Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: 5/119; al-Sunan al-Kubrā: 8/175, with variation.]

And who says: "I will send down the like of what God has sent down."

It was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ al-Qurashī, who used to write for the Prophet (ﷺ). Whenever he wrote "Samīʿan ʿAlīman," he would write "ʿAlīman Ḥakīman," and when he wrote "ʿAlīman Ḥakīman," he would write "Ghafūran Raḥīman," and similar things. When God revealed "And We created man from an extract of clay" [Surah al-Mu'minun: 12], up to the verse—

The Prophet (ﷺ) dictated it, and ʿAbd Allāh was amazed at the detail of the creation of man, and said: "Blessed is God, the best of creators." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Write it down, for thus was it revealed."

[Tafsir al-Qurṭubī: 7/40, where it reads: "and thus was it revealed to me."]

Then ʿAbd Allāh doubted and said: "If Muhammad is truthful, then it was revealed to me as it was revealed to him; and if he is lying, then I have said [as he wrote]." [Thus in the original.] He apostatized from the Muslims and joined the polytheists, and he said to them: "Follow Muhammad; he used to dictate to me, and I would alter it and write as I wished."

Ibn Abī Sarḥ also informed on ʿAmmār and Jubayr, a slave of the Banū al-Ḥaḍramī, and they seized them and tortured them until they gave them unbelief. ʿAmmār's ear was cut off that day. ʿAmmār informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of what he had suffered and of what he had given them of disbelief, but the Prophet (ﷺ) refused that these people should be his guardians, so God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed concerning him:

In another report, and Ibn Abī Sarḥ: "Whoever disbelieves in God after his faith—" up to His words "with disbelief."

This refers to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ, who then returned to Islam before the conquest of Mecca, when the Prophet (ﷺ) [descended with Mirṭ Harān].

And if you could see when the wrongdoers (al-ẓālimūn), namely those whom God mentioned and described before, are in the agonies of death (ghamarāt al-mawt), its pangs. Ghamarāt is the plural of ghamra, and the ghamra of everything is its abundance and greatest part; and the root meaning is the thing that covers things and overwhelms them, and from it comes "the flood of water"; then it was used for hardships and calamities. The angels stretch forth their hands (bāsiṭū aydīhim), with punishment and blows, toward their faces and their backs, as one says "he stretched out his hand with harm." "Bring out" (akhrijū): that is, they say: "Bring out your souls (anfusakum), your spirits, against your will," for the soul of the believer is eager to go out to meet its Lord. The answer is omitted, meaning: if you could see them in this state, you would see a marvel.

"Today you will be recompensed (tujzawna) with the punishment of humiliation (ʿadhāb al-hawn), that is, the humiliation, for what you used to say against God other than the truth, and for being arrogant (tastakbirūn) toward His signs"—meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an—"you used to magnify yourselves."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prostrates to God one prostration, he is free from pride."

[Kanz al-ʿUmmāl: 7/308.]

"And you have come to Us alone (furādā), as We created you the first time, naked, barefoot, uncircumcised." This is a report from God, Exalted, that He will say to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection: "And you have come to Us alone (furādā), singly, with no wealth with you, no spouse, no child, no servants, no retinue."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 6, verse 95–99:

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone.﴾ That is, He splits the grain to bring forth plants, and brings out the crop from it; and He splits the date-stone to bring forth trees and palms, and brings them out from it.

Mujahid said: It means the two splits that he mentioned.

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-stone.﴾ "Grain" (habb) is the plural of habba, which is everything that has no stone, such as wheat, barley, millet and all grains.

"Date-stones" (nawa) is the plural of nawāh (stone), which is everything that has a pit, such as peaches, apricots, dates, plums and the like.

﴿He brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded?﴾ That is, how are you turned away from the truth?

﴿Splitter of the daybreak﴾ (fāliq al-iṣbāḥ): He cleaves the column of dawn out of the darkness of night and reveals it.

Al-Dahhak said: "Creator of the day." Al-iṣbāḥ is a verbal noun like al-iqbāl and al-idbār, and it means illumination.

Al-Hasan and al-Qaysi read fālaq al-iṣbāḥ with a fatḥa on the hamza, taking it as a plural like qarṣ and aqrāṣ.

﴿And He made the night a resting-place﴾ (sakan): He made people rest in it. Al-Nakha'i read: falaqa al-aṣbāḥ wa ja'ala al-layla sakanan.

The people of Kufa read: fālaqa al-iṣbāḥi wa ja'ala al-layla sakanan, in the verbal form, following the Mushaf.

The rest read both with alif, in the noun form.

﴿And the sun and the moon [as] a reckoning﴾ (ḥusbānan): that is, He made the sun and the moon by a reckoning that they do not exceed, until they reach their furthest stations.

Yazid ibn Qa'nab read: wa al-shamsi wa al-qamari with a kasra, in agreement with the wording (al-lafz). Ḥusbān is a verbal noun like nuqsān and Raḥmān, and it may also be the plural of ḥisāb, like shihāb and shihbān, and rikāb and rukbān.

﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ And He it is who made for you the stars, that is, created them, ﴿so that you may be guided by them in the darkness of the land and the sea.﴾ ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who know.﴾ And He it is who produced you, created and originated you ﴿from a single soul﴾, meaning Adam (ʿalayhi al-salam).

﴿fa-mustaqarr﴾: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read fa-mustaqirr with a kasra on the qaf, as an active participle, meaning: for you there is a place of settlement.

The rest read it with a fatha, in the sense: for you there is a place of settlement.

The exegetes differed concerning al-mustaqarr and al-mustawda'. ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿mustaqarr﴾ is in the womb until it is entrusted (to the world); ﴿mustawda'﴾ is in the grave until resurrection.

Muqatil said: mustaqarr is where it settles, and mustawda' is where it dies.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: mustaqarr is in the wombs of mothers, and mustawda' is in the loins of fathers.

He also said: Ibn ʿAbbas (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) said to me, "Have you married, O son of Jubayr?" I said, "No, and I have no intention of that at all." He struck my back and said, "Whatever is deposited in your loins will certainly come out."

ʿIkrima reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: al-mustaqarr is that which has been created and settled in the womb, and al-mustawda' is that which has been deposited in the loins and not yet created, and He is its Creator.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talha reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: al-mustaqarr is in the womb, and al-mustawda' is what is deposited in the loins of men and animals.

Mujahid: ﴿mustaqarr﴾ is on the surface of the earth in this world; ﴿mustawda'﴾ is with Allah, the Exalted, in the Hereafter.

Abu al-ʿAliya said: mustaqarrahā is its days of life, and mustawda'ahā is where it dies and where it is raised.

ʿIkrima reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: al-mustaqarr is that which has been created and settled in the womb, and al-mustawda' is that which has been deposited in the loins and not yet created, and He is its Creator.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talha reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: al-mustaqarr is in the womb, and al-mustawda' is what is deposited in the loins of men and animals.

Mujahid: ﴿mustaqarr﴾ is on the surface of the earth in this world; ﴿mustawda'﴾ is with Allah, the Exalted, in the Hereafter.

Abu al-ʿAliya said: mustaqarrahā is its days of life, and mustawda'ahā is where it dies and where it is raised.

Karib said: Ibn ʿAbbas (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) called me and said: "Write: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. From ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas to so-and-so, the scholar of Taymaʾ. To proceed: tell me about mustaqarr and mustawda'." He then sent me with the letter to a Jew, and I gave it to him. He said, "Welcome to the letter of my friend among the Muslims," and went to his house, opened many of his chests, and began to throw aside those things without looking at them. I said to him, "What is the matter with you?" He said, "These are things the Jews have written," until he brought out the Book of Moses and looked at it twice, then said: "Mustaqarr is in the womb; mustaqarr is above the earth; mustaqarr is under the earth; and mustaqarr is where it goes, to Paradise or to Hell." Then he recited: ﴿And We cause to settle in the wombs what We will﴾, and he recited: ﴿And for you on the earth is a place of settlement and provision for a time﴾ [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/377.]].

Al-Hasan read: al-mustaqarr is in the grave, and al-mustawda' is in this world, and he used to say: "O son of Adam, you are a deposit with your family; you will soon join your companion." He recited the verse of Labid:

"And wealth and family are only a deposit, and deposits must one day be returned."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 8/190.]]

Sulayman ibn Yazid al-ʿAdawi said on this meaning:

"So He gathered the beloved with the beloved before us,
and people are bereaved by them and bereave."

"Whether one enters as a deposit or as a settled one, the settled one is visited by the deposited one."
[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 4/120.]]

﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who understand.﴾ And He it is who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth with it, with the water, the vegetation of every thing; then We brought forth from it, from the water, and it was said: from the vegetation, green (khaḍiran), meaning green, which is the moist herbage. He says: it is for you green and wholesome, that is, pleasant and wholesome.

Nakhla said: khaḍīra is when a tree casts its unripe dates green before they ripen. It is said: "ikhtaḍara" and "ightaḍara" for a man who dies young while in health [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/380.]].

﴿And from the palm, from its spathe, [come] clusters of dates﴾: that is, its fruit; [and many of them], and what sprouts from them. Qinwān is the plural of qinw, which is the bunch, like ṣinw and ṣinwān.

Abu ʿUbayda said: [there is no harm in this expression].

Al-Aʿraj read qunwān with a ḍamma on the qaf, which is the dialect of Qays, like quḍbān. The dialect of Tamim is qiniyān. Its paucal plural is aqnā, like ḥinw and aḥnā. ﴿Near﴾ (dāniyah): close, within reach of the one standing or sitting. Mujahid said: hanging down.

Qatada said: drooping [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/382.]].

Al-Dahhak said: short ones, clinging to the ground. [[Attributed in Zad al-Masir (3/65) to Ibn ʿAbbas with the wording: the short palms whose clusters reach the ground.]] The meaning of the verse is: from the palms come clusters near at hand, and others that are far; he mentioned only the near ones and omitted the far, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl: 81.]], and the cold. ﴿And gardens﴾, meaning: and We brought forth from it gardens.

Yahya ibn Yaʿmur, al-Aʿmash and ʿAsim read: ﴿wa jannātun﴾ in the nominative, coordinated with qinwān in wording, though not in meaning being of its kind: ﴿of grapes, and olives and pomegranates﴾, meaning and the trees of olives and pomegranates. He mentioned the palm and omitted the other trees, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [[Surah Yusuf: 82.]], ﴿resembling one another and not resembling﴾. Qatada: its leaves resemble one another while its fruit differs. It is also said: resembling in appearance, not resembling in taste. Al-Hasan said: some of its kinds resemble one another and some differ. It is also said: resembling in creation, from its origin, from wisdom. ﴿Look at its fruit﴾.

The people of Kufa read: with a ḍamma on the thā' and the mīm, as the plural of thimār (fruits). The rest read with a fatḥa on both, as the plural of thamara, like ba'r and wabr. ﴿When it bears fruit﴾ (idhā athmara), ﴿and its ripening﴾ (yani'ihi): its maturing and ripeness.

Abu Raja' and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read: wa yāni'ahu with an alif, in the noun form. ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 6, verse 95–99:

Mujahid said: It means the two splits that he mentioned.

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-stone.﴾ "Grain" (habb) is the plural of habba, which is everything that has no stone, such as wheat, barley, millet and all grains.

"Date-stones" (nawa) is the plural of nawāh (stone), which is everything that has a pit, such as peaches, apricots, dates, plums and the like.

﴿He brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded?﴾ That is, how are you turned away from the truth?

﴿Splitter of the daybreak﴾ (fāliq al-iṣbāḥ): He cleaves the column of dawn out of the darkness of night and reveals it.

Al-Dahhak said: "Creator of the day." Al-iṣbāḥ is a verbal noun like al-iqbāl and al-idbār, and it means illumination.

Al-Hasan and al-Qaysi read fālaq al-iṣbāḥ with a fatḥa on the hamza, taking it as a plural like qarṣ and aqrāṣ.

﴿And He made the night a resting-place﴾ (sakan): He made people rest in it. Al-Nakha'i read: falaqa al-aṣbāḥ wa ja'ala al-layla sakanan.

The people of Kufa read: fālaqa al-iṣbāḥi wa ja'ala al-layla sakanan, in the verbal form, following the Mushaf.

The rest read both with alif, in the noun form.

﴿And the sun and the moon [as] a reckoning﴾ (ḥusbānan): that is, He made the sun and the moon by a reckoning that they do not exceed, until they reach their furthest stations.

Yazid ibn Qa'nab read: wa al-shamsi wa al-qamari with a kasra, in agreement with the wording (al-lafz). Ḥusbān is a verbal noun like nuqsān and Raḥmān, and it may also be the plural of ḥisāb, like shihāb and shihbān, and rikāb and rukbān.

﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ And He it is who made for you the stars, that is, created them, ﴿so that you may be guided by them in the darkness of the land and the sea.﴾ ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who know.﴾ And He it is who produced you, created and originated you ﴿from a single soul﴾, meaning Adam (ʿalayhi al-salam).

The rest read it with a fatha, in the sense: for you there is a place of settlement.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 6, verses 100–107:

The disbelievers "made the jinn partners with Allah" (وَجَعَلُوا لِلَّهِ شُرَكاءَ الْجِنَّ). That is, they made the jinn partners of Allah. If you wish, you may read "al-jinn" in the accusative as an explanatory substitute (tafsir) for "shuraka'" (partners). "And He created them": that is, He created them and He created the jinn.

Yahya ibn Mu'ammar read وَخَلْقَهُمْ with a sukun on the lam and a fatha on the qaf. He meant their lie and their claim regarding the idols they worshipped, in that they made them partners with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning is: "and they attributed to Him their own creation."

Yahya ibn Wathhab read وَخَلْقِهِمْ with a sukun on the lam and a kasra on the qaf. The meaning: they made partners for Allah, and they associated them with Allah in His creation of them.

Al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning the zanadiqa (heretics), who said: "Allah and Iblis are two partners. Allah created the light, the people, the animals and the cattle, while Iblis created the darkness, the beasts of prey, the scorpions and the snakes." This is like His saying: "And they made between Him and the jinn a kinship" (وَجَعَلُوا بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ الْجِنَّةِ نَسَباً), meaning in Paradise. The jinn (al-jinnah) are a class of angels, the guardians of the gardens, and a class of jinn was said to be their kin. "And they invented" (وَخَرَقُوا), that is, they fabricated and conjectured.

The people of Madina read بِكَثْرَةٍ "and they invented" with intensive emphasis (خَرَّقُوا). "For Him sons and daughters without knowledge" (لَهُ بَنِينَ وَبَناتٍ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ). These were the disbelievers of Makka, who said: "The angels and the idols are the daughters of Allah." The Jews said: "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah." Then He declared His own transcendence: "Glory be to Him, and high is He above what they describe. The Originator of the heavens and the earth: how could He have a son when He has no consort (ṣāḥiba), that is, a wife, and He created all things, and He is Knowing of all things."

Regarding His saying "Vision cannot perceive Him" (لا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصارُ), some scholars took it in its general sense and said: its meaning is that the eyes do not encompass Him, but they see Him while He encompasses them [see Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/54].

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "And they cannot encompass Him in knowledge" (وَلا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْماً). Just as you know Him in this world without knowing Him as one knows the known things, so you will see Him in the Hereafter without seeing Him as one sees the seen things.

They said: One may see a thing without perceiving it, as Allah related about the companions of Musa (peace be upon him) when Fir'awn drew near them: "Indeed, we are overtaken" (إِنَّا لَمُدْرَكُونَ). The people of Fir'awn had seen the people of Musa but did not overtake them, because Allah had promised His prophet Musa (peace be upon him) that they would not overtake them, by His saying: "Do not fear being overtaken, nor be apprehensive" (لا تَخافُ دَرَكاً وَلا تَخْشى).

Likewise, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "The eyes do not encompass Him." 'Ata' said: "The eyes of created beings are unable to encompass Him." Al-Hasan said: "The eyes do not fall upon Him, the intellects do not reach Him, and certitude does not comprehend Him."

This is supported by what 'Ata'iyya al-'Awfi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying "Vision cannot perceive Him, but He perceives vision" (لا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصارُ وَهُوَ يُدْرِكُ الْأَبْصارَ). He said: "If the jinn, the humans, the devils and the angels, from the time they were created until they perish, were to stand in one row, they would never encompass Allah."

[See Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/167.]

Others took it in its literal sense. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: its meaning is that "vision cannot perceive Him" in this world, but He is seen in the Hereafter. "And He perceives vision" (وَهُوَ يُدْرِكُ الْأَبْصارَ): nothing is hidden from Him and nothing escapes Him.

It was said: its meaning is that the eyes of the disbelievers cannot perceive Him, but the believers will see Him, and Allah knows best. "And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware" (وَهُوَ اللَّطِيفُ الْخَبِيرُ).

Abu al-'Aliya said: "Subtle" means extracting things, and "All-Aware" means knowing them.

Most scholars spoke about the meaning of al-Latif. Al-Junayd said: "Al-Latif is He who illuminates your heart with guidance, nourishes your body with food, grants you authority in trials, guards you from the blazing fire, and admits you to the Garden of Refuge."

It was said: al-Latif is He who makes His servants forget their sins so that they are not shamed. It was said: He is the One who formed man from a drop, "from a despised water" (مِنْ ماءٍ مَهِينٍ). It was said: He is the One who regards His abundant blessings as little and regards the little obedience of His servants as much.

Qatada said: It was said: al-Latif is the One who changes but is not changed. It was said: al-Latif is the One who, if you hope in Him, responds to you; if you aim for Him, shelters you; if you love Him, brings you near; if you obey Him, suffices you; if you disobey Him, pardons you; if you turn away from Him, calls you; and if you turn toward Him, draws near to you.

It was said: al-Latif is the One who does not seek from His beloved their lineage or ancestry. It was said: al-Latif is the One who makes the poor who depend on Him wealthy and honors the proud who take pride in Him. It was said: al-Latif is the One who rewards the one who fulfills and pardons the one who falls short. It was said:

al-Latif is the One whose commands bring nearness and whose prohibitions bring discipline.

It was said: al-Latif is the One whose giving is good and whose withholding is a treasure. The root of al-latif is fineness of perception regarding all things.

"Indeed, there have come to you clear proofs from your Lord" (قَدْ جاءَكُمْ بَصائِرُ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ), meaning the clear arguments by which they see guidance from error and truth from falsehood.

Al-Kalbi said: this means the clear verses of the Qur'an.

"So whoever sees" (فَمَنْ أَبْصَرَ), meaning recognizes them and believes in them, "benefits himself" (فَلِنَفْسِهِ), his work and his portion is attained, and for it he seeks good. "And whoever is blind" (وَمَنْ عَمِيَ), meaning he is blind to them, so he neither recognizes nor affirms them, "then it is against himself" (فَعَلَيْها).

Talha ibn Musarrif read وَمَنْ عُمِّيَ with a damma on the 'ayn and a shadda on the meem, in the passive form, the implied subject being the one who is blinded. The meaning: "then his own self bears the harm, and to it he has done wrong, not to anyone else." "And I am not a guardian over you" (وَما أَنَا عَلَيْكُمْ بِحَفِيظٍ), that is, a watcher who counts your deeds against you. "I am only a messenger who conveys to you the messages of my Lord," and He is the Guardian over you, from whom none of your actions is hidden.

"And thus We vary the verses" (وَكَذلِكَ نُصَرِّفُ الْآياتِ), that is, We explain them in every way, so that We may call you by them. "And so that they may say" (وَلِيَقُولُوا), lest they say when you recite the Qur'an to them: "You have studied" (دَرَسْتَ), that is, you have recited and read, O Muhammad, without an alif. This was read by a group including Abu Raja', Abu Wa'il, al-A'raj, and most of the people of Iraq and the Hijaz. 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr used to say: "Children recite it as dārasta with an alif, but it is only darasta."

'Ali, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read دَارَسْتَ with an alif, meaning: you studied with the People of the Book and learned from them, and they recited to you so that you might recite to them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means you disputed and argued, and so he used to read it. Qatada read دُرِسَتْ, meaning "it was recited and read."

Al-Hasan, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read دَرَسَتْ with a fatha on the dal and the ra' and a sukun on the ta', meaning "it has become old and effaced." Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Talha and al-A'mash read دَرَسَ with a fatha on it, meaning: the Prophet "effaced the verses," that is, he taught them.

"And that We may make it clear" (وَلِنُبَيِّنَهُ), that is, the statement, the alteration and the Qur'an, "for a people who know" (لِقَوْمٍ يَعْلَمُونَ).

"Follow, O Muhammad, what is revealed to you from your Lord" (اتَّبِعْ ما أُوحِيَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ), that is, the Qur'an. Act upon it. "There is no god but Him" (لا إِلهَ إِلَّا هُوَ), "and turn away from the polytheists" (وَأَعْرِضْ عَنِ الْمُشْرِكِينَ), that is, do not dispute with them and do not punish them.

"If Allah had willed, they would not have associated others" (وَلَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ ما أَشْرَكُوا), "and We have not made you a guardian over them" (وَما جَعَلْناكَ عَلَيْهِمْ حَفِيظاً), that is, a watcher. It is also said: a guardian.

'Ata' said: "We have not made you a guardian over them" means you do not protect them from Me, "and you are not a trustee over them" (وَما أَنْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِوَكِيلٍ). The command to turn away is abrogated by the verse of the sword. This verse was revealed when the polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Return to the religion of your fathers."

Yahya ibn Wathhab read وَخَلْقِهِمْ with a sukun on the lam and a kasra on the qaf. The meaning: they made partners for Allah, and they associated them with Allah in His creation of them.

Al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning the zanadiqa (heretics), who said: "Allah and Iblis are two partners. Allah created the light, the people, the animals and the cattle, while Iblis created the darkness, the beasts of prey, the scorpions and the snakes." This is like His saying: "And they made between Him and the jinn a kinship" (وَجَعَلُوا بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ الْجِنَّةِ نَسَباً), meaning in Paradise. The jinn (al-jinnah) are a class of angels, the guardians of the gardens, and a class of jinn was said to be their kin. "And they invented" (وَخَرَقُوا), that is, they fabricated and conjectured.

The people of Madina read بِكَثْرَةٍ "and they invented" with intensive emphasis (خَرَّقُوا). "For Him sons and daughters without knowledge" (لَهُ بَنِينَ وَبَناتٍ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ). These were the disbelievers of Makka, who said: "The angels and the idols are the daughters of Allah." The Jews said: "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah." Then He declared His own transcendence: "Glory be to Him, and high is He above what they describe. The Originator of the heavens and the earth: how could He have a son when He has no consort (ṣāḥiba), that is, a wife, and He created all things, and He is Knowing of all things."

Regarding His saying "Vision cannot perceive Him" (لا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصارُ), some scholars took it in its general sense and said: its meaning is that the eyes do not encompass Him, but they see Him while He encompasses them [see Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/54].

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "And they cannot encompass Him in knowledge" (وَلا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْماً). Just as you know Him in this world without knowing Him as one knows the known things, so you will see Him in the Hereafter without seeing Him as one sees the seen things.

They said: One may see a thing without perceiving it, as Allah related about the companions of Musa (peace be upon him) when Fir'awn drew near them: "Indeed, we are overtaken" (إِنَّا لَمُدْرَكُونَ). The people of Fir'awn had seen the people of Musa but did not overtake them, because Allah had promised His prophet Musa (peace be upon him) that they would not overtake them, by His saying: "Do not fear being overtaken, nor be apprehensive" (لا تَخافُ دَرَكاً وَلا تَخْشى).

Likewise, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "The eyes do not encompass Him." 'Ata' said: "The eyes of created beings are unable to encompass Him." Al-Hasan said: "The eyes do not fall upon Him, the intellects do not reach Him, and certitude does not comprehend Him."

This is supported by what 'Ata'iyya al-'Awfi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying "Vision cannot perceive Him, but He perceives vision" (لا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصارُ وَهُوَ يُدْرِكُ الْأَبْصارَ). He said: "If the jinn, the humans, the devils and the angels, from the time they were created until they perish, were to stand in one row, they would never encompass Allah."

[See Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/167.]

Others took it in its literal sense. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: its meaning is that "vision cannot perceive Him" in this world, but He is seen in the Hereafter. "And He perceives vision" (وَهُوَ يُدْرِكُ الْأَبْصارَ): nothing is hidden from Him and nothing escapes Him.

It was said: its meaning is that the eyes of the disbelievers cannot perceive Him, but the believers will see Him, and Allah knows best. "And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware" (وَهُوَ اللَّطِيفُ الْخَبِيرُ).

Abu al-'Aliya said: "Subtle" means extracting things, and "All-Aware" means knowing them.

Most scholars spoke about the meaning of al-Latif. Al-Junayd said: "Al-Latif is He who illuminates your heart with guidance, nourishes your body with food, grants you authority in trials, guards you from the blazing fire, and admits you to the Garden of Refuge."

It was said: al-Latif is He who makes His servants forget their sins so that they are not shamed. It was said: He is the One who formed man from a drop, "from a despised water" (مِنْ ماءٍ مَهِينٍ). It was said: He is the One who regards His abundant blessings as little and regards the little obedience of His servants as much.

Qatada said: It was said: al-Latif is the One who changes but is not changed. It was said: al-Latif is the One who, if you hope in Him, responds to you; if you aim for Him, shelters you; if you love Him, brings you near; if you obey Him, suffices you; if you disobey Him, pardons you; if you turn away from Him, calls you; and if you turn toward Him, draws near to you.

It was said: al-Latif is the One who does not seek from His beloved their lineage or ancestry. It was said: al-Latif is the One who makes the poor who depend on Him wealthy and honors the proud who take pride in Him. It was said: al-Latif is the One who rewards the one who fulfills and pardons the one who falls short. It was said:

al-Latif is the One whose commands bring nearness and whose prohibitions bring discipline.

It was said: al-Latif is the One whose giving is good and whose withholding is a treasure. The root of al-latif is fineness of perception regarding all things.

"Indeed, there have come to you clear proofs from your Lord" (قَدْ جاءَكُمْ بَصائِرُ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ), meaning the clear arguments by which they see guidance from error and truth from falsehood.

Al-Kalbi said: this means the clear verses of the Qur'an.

"So whoever sees" (فَمَنْ أَبْصَرَ), meaning recognizes them and believes in them, "benefits himself" (فَلِنَفْسِهِ), his work and his portion is attained, and for it he seeks good. "And whoever is blind" (وَمَنْ عَمِيَ), meaning he is blind to them, so he neither recognizes nor affirms them, "then it is against himself" (فَعَلَيْها).

The meaning: "then his own self bears the harm, and to it he has done wrong, not to anyone else." "And I am not a guardian over you" (وَما أَنَا عَلَيْكُمْ بِحَفِيظٍ), that is, a watcher who counts your deeds against you. "I am only a messenger who conveys to you the messages of my Lord," and He is the Guardian over you, from whom none of your actions is hidden.

"And thus We vary the verses" (وَكَذلِكَ نُصَرِّفُ الْآياتِ), that is, We explain them in every way, so that We may call you by them. This was read by a group including Abu Raja', Abu Wa'il, al-A'raj, and most of the people of Iraq and the Hijaz. 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr used to say: "Children recite it as dārasta with an alif, but it is only darasta."

'Ali, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read دَارَسْتَ with an alif, meaning: you studied with the People of the Book and learned from them, and they recited to you so that you might recite to them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means you disputed and argued, and so he used to read it. Qatada read دُرِسَتْ, meaning "it was recited and read."

Al-Hasan, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read دَرَسَتْ with a fatha on the dal and the ra' and a sukun on the ta', meaning "it has become old and effaced." Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Talha and al-A'mash read دَرَسَ with a fatha on it, meaning: the Prophet "effaced the verses," that is, he taught them.

"And that We may make it clear" (وَلِنُبَيِّنَهُ), that is, the statement, the alteration and the Qur'an, "for a people who know" (لِقَوْمٍ يَعْلَمُونَ).

"Follow, O Muhammad, what is revealed to you from your Lord" (اتَّبِعْ ما أُوحِيَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ), that is, the Qur'an. Act upon it.
