When what they had designated for their associates perished or was barren, and what was for God increased, they said: "Our gods must have their expenditure." So they took what was for God and spent it on their gods. When what was for God was barren and what was for their gods increased, they said: "If God had willed, He would have made pure what was His," and they would not return anything of what belonged to the gods. When drought struck them, they sought help from what they had set apart, and gathered for their associates what they set apart. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of what He has produced of the tilth and the cattle a portion﴾, that is, of what He has left over from the tilth and the cattle a portion. There is an implied ellipsis here, its meaning being: they assigned to God a portion and to their associates a portion.

﴿They say: "This is for God," by their claim﴾.

Yahya ibn Ri'ab, al-Sulami, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i recited it with a damma. The rest recited it with a fatha. Both are dialectal forms, and it means a saying without reality.

I heard al-Husayn say: I heard al-Anbari relate from Abu al-Abbas al-Azhari from Abu Hatim that he said:
Shurayh the judge said: "Indeed everything has a kunya (figurative name), and the kunya of falsehood is 'they claim' (za'amu). And zaim also means greed."

﴿And this is for our associates﴾, meaning the idols. ﴿But what is for their associates does not reach God, while what is for God reaches their associates.﴾ ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾, that is: wretched is what they were deciding.

﴿And thus did their associates make attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾: just as they made attractive to them the prohibition of the tilth and the cattle, so too they made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children. ﴿Their associates﴾, meaning their devils, adorned and beautified it for them, namely burying daughters alive out of fear of poverty.

al-Kalbi said: "Their associates" are the custodians (sadana) of their idols, and they are the ones who used to make the killing of their children attractive to the disbelievers. A man in the Jahiliyya would swear by God that if a son were born to him, he would surely slaughter one of them, just as Abd al-Muttalib swore concerning his son Abd Allah. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/91.]

The people of Syria recited zuyyina with a damma, qatlu in the nominative, awladihim in the accusative, and shurakaihim in the genitive by way of advancement, as if he said: "He made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their associates' children." They thereby separated the verb from its agent.

A poet says:
"He passes over what passes, and the garments have been torn, not the self, their chests"
He means: shaqqat (were torn).
The tribe of Abd al-Qays: "ghalail suduruha" (the garments of their chests).

Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited zuyyina with a damma on the zay, qatlu in the nominative, awladihim in the genitive, and shurakauhum in the nominative by way of "al-tawdih" and repetition. [The text here reads "al-tawdih," as in the original.]

As if, when He said: "He made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children," the statement was complete; then He said: "By whom was it made attractive?" And He said: "Their associates," meaning their associates made it attractive. So the associates are raised by a verb of a pronoun indicated by zuyyina, as you say: "The meat was eaten by Zayd," as if it were said: "Who is the eater?" and you say: "Zayd."

A poet says:
"Let him weep for Zayd, the one who is afflicted by a dispute, and the one who is struck by what the calamities strike down."
So Zayd is an object standing by itself, whose agent is not named; then he explained it by saying: "ḍāri'," meaning: let the one afflicted weep for him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to ruin them﴾, that is, to destroy them; ﴿and to confuse them﴾, that is, to mix up and make ambiguous for them ﴿their religion﴾. They had been upon the religion of Ismail, but they turned away from it. ﴿And had God willed, they would not have done it﴾, that is, had God willed, He would have guided them, granted them success and preserved them from doing that prohibition of the cattle and the tilth. It was also said: "the children." ﴿So leave them, O Muhammad, and what they fabricate﴾, that is, what they invent against God of falsehood, for God is ever watchful over them and ﴿will not fail His promise﴾.

﴿And they say﴾, meaning the polytheists: ﴿These are cattle and tilth, forbidden﴾, meaning what they had assigned to God and to their gods, which has already been mentioned. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/59.]

Mujahid said: By "cattle" he means the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham. "Hijr" means forbidden. God said: ﴿and they say, "a forbidden barrier"﴾ (al-Furqan 25:22), that is, forbidden and prohibited.

al-Layth said:
"She longed for the farthest palm, so I said to her: 'Forbidden, forbidden; behold those are the rugged lands.'" [Kitab al-'Ayn: 4/120; Lisan al-'Arab: 6/90; the verse is attributed to Jarir, and is also narrated as "hajjat."]

Its origin is from hajr, which means prevention and prohibition, and from it: the judge's restriction (hajr) of a wrongdoer.

al-Hasan and Qatadah recited wa-harthun hujr with a damma on the ha', both being dialectal forms. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Talha and al-A'mash recited wa-harthun harj with a kasra on the ha' and a ra' before the jim; this is also a dialect, like jadhab and jabadh.

Abu Amr recited:
"Did you not kill the two harijin when they appeared to you, passing by with hands of tough, braided bark?" [Lisan al-'Arab: 2/236; the verse is by al-Hudhali.]

﴿None shall eat of it except whom we will﴾, according to their claim. They mean men without women. ﴿And cattle whose backs are forbidden﴾ means the ham, when its offspring's offspring rides. They said: "He has protected its back, so it is not ridden nor carried upon." ﴿And cattle over which they do not mention the name of God﴾.

Mujahid said: among their cattle there was a group over which they did not mention the name of God, nor in anything concerning them: neither when they rode them, nor when they milked them, nor when they birthed them, nor when they sold them, nor when they carried loads on them.

Abu Asim said: Abu Wa'il said to me: "Do you know what 'cattle whose backs are forbidden' means?" I said: "No." He said: "They do not perform the hajj upon them."

al-Dahhak said: they are those which, when they slaughtered them, they invoked their idols over them. ﴿And over which they do not mention the name of God﴾, fabricating against Him. That is, they used to do that and claimed that God had commanded them to it. ﴿He will recompense them for what they used to fabricate.﴾

﴿And they say: "What is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males"﴾.

Ibn Abbas, al-Sha'bi and Qatadah said: it means the milk of the slaughtered-for-idols animals was for the males and not for the women; when it died, its meat was shared by their males and females.

al-Suddi said: it means the offspring of the slaughtered-for-idols animals: a portion exclusively for the man and not for the women; [but what is born dead, that is eaten by] men and women. The ta' in khalisatun was added for emphasis and intensification, as it was done with rawiyah, nassabah and 'allamah.

al-Farra' said: the ta' was added because of the feminine gender of the cattle, since what is in its belly is like it, so it was made feminine by its femininity. He said: khalisah may also be like 'aqibah. Among its instances is His saying: ﴿Indeed We purified them with an exclusive remembrance of the abode﴾ (Sad 38:46). Abdullah and al-A'mash recited khalis li-dhukurina without the ta', referring it back to ma. Ibn Abbas recited khalisatun in the construct form, and khalisah, khuliyasah and khalsan are one and the same. The poet says:
"I was my confidant, and I was my exclusive one, and not every man is trustworthy."
[This line is from verses composed by Sulayman ibn Qatta lamenting Imam al-Hasan (peace be upon him), as in Sharh Nahj al-Balagha by Ibn Abi al-Hadid: 6/52, where the second half reads instead: "For every living one there is a dwelling among his people."]

﴿And forbidden to our wives﴾, meaning the women. ﴿And if it should be dead﴾: Ahl al-Madina recited takun with the ta', and mayta with a damma, meaning: if the cattle should become dead. The people of Mecca recited yakun with the ya', and mayta with a damma, meaning: if what is in the bellies of the cattle should become dead. al-A'mash recited takun with the ta' and mayta with a fatha, meaning: if it should be [what is in the bellies of the cattle is dead]. [Addition from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/96.] The rest recited yakun with the ya' and mayta with a fatha, referring it to what supports this: His saying ﴿then they are partners in it﴾, and He did not say "in them." ﴿He will recompense them for their description﴾, that is, for their description and their claim of falsehood against God, like His saying: ﴿and their tongues describe the lie﴾ (al-Nahl 16:62). Wasf and sifah are one, like wizn and zinah, and wa'd and 'idah. ﴿Indeed, He is Wise, Knowing.﴾

﴿Certainly, those have lost who killed their children in foolishness﴾, the verse was revealed concerning Rabi'ah and Mudar, and concerning the Arabs who buried their daughters alive out of fear of captivity and poverty, except for the Banu Kinanah, for they did not do that.

Abu Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, the people of Mecca and Syria recited qatthalu with an emphatic doubled tა' for intensification; the rest recited it lightly. ﴿Without knowledge﴾, ﴿and they have prohibited what God provided them﴾, meaning the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham, ﴿fabricating against God﴾ when they said that God commanded them with it. ﴿They have certainly gone astray and were not guided.﴾

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 6, verses 141–144:**

﴿And it is He who produced﴾ means He invented and originated ﴿gardens﴾, meaning orchards,

﴿trellised and untrellised﴾, meaning raised up and not raised up. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿trellised﴾ refers to what spreads over the surface of the earth and sprawls, from what is trained, such as the grapevine, the gourd, the watermelon and others. ﴿Untrellised﴾ refers to what stands on a stalk, such as date palms and the rest of the trees, and what grows in a row, and like [the (?) ...]. Al-Dahhak said: ﴿trellised and untrellised﴾ refers specifically to the grapevine: some of it is trellised and some of it is not trellised.

It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas that the trellised ones are those that people train (i.e., raise up their branches), and the untrellised ones are those that grow in the wilderness and mountains of fruits. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/69.]

Evidence for this is the reading of Ali: (mughrusat wa-ghayr mughrusat), with the letters ghayn and sin (i.e., "planted" rather than "trellised").

﴿And the palm trees﴾, meaning and He produced the palm trees, ﴿and the crops, varying in their produce﴾, meaning their fruit and taste: sour, bitter, sweet, good and bad. The meaning of "food" (ukul) is raised (as the subject), except that since the qualifier (mukhtalifan, "varying") preceded the noun and followed as an accusative, it took the accusative case, just as you say: "'indi tabbakhan ghulam" (I have a cook, a boy). And a poet recited:

"Evil is spread out to meet you [from illness], and good deeds have a door closed upon them."

﴿And the olive and the pomegranate, similar in appearance and dissimilar in taste﴾, like two pomegranates whose color is one but whose taste differs: one sweet and the other sour. This has been discussed before. ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit, and do not forbid it as the people of ignorance did﴾, ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾. The people of Mecca, Medina and Kufa read ḥiṣādihi with a kasra on the ḥa, and the others with a fatḥa; both are the same, like jidad (cutting/harvesting). Al-jidad, al-ṣaram and al-ṣiram [are the same]. The scholars differed concerning the ruling of this verse. Ibn Abbas, Tawus, al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: [it is the obligatory zakat], the tenth and the half-tenth.

Ali ibn al-Husayn, Ata, Hammad and al-Hakam said: it is a right in wealth other than zakat.

Mujahid said: when you reap and the poor come to you, cast some of the spikes for them; when you cut the stalks, leave for them some of the pods; when you thresh and winnow it, cast some of it for them; when you pile it and clean it, cast some of it for them; and when you know its measure, set aside its zakat.

Ibrahim said: it is the handful (daghth). Al-Rabi' said: the gleanings of the spikes. Mujahid said: they used to hang a cluster of dates at the time of harvesting, so that the guest and whoever passed by would eat from it.

Zayd ibn al-Asamm said: the people of [ignorance], when they harvested, would bring the cluster and hang it on the side of the mosque; a poor man would come and strike it with his stick, so some of it would fall, and he would take it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ata said: this was before zakat; when zakat was prescribed, this was abrogated (naskh).

Sufyan and al-Suddi said: I asked about this verse, and he said: "It was abrogated by the tenth and the half-tenth." I said: "By whom?" He said: "By the scholars." Muqatil [narrated] from Ibn Abbas: "Zakat abrogated every charity mentioned in the Qur'an."

﴿And do not be extravagant; indeed He does not love the extravagant﴾. Some men used to spend it on what was forbidden; a man would say, "I will not withhold from a beggar until evening." Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas went to five hundred palm trees, cut them, and distributed them all in one day, leaving nothing for his family. So the verse was revealed: "and do not be extravagant," meaning do not give all of it. Al-Suddi said: "do not be extravagant" means do not give away your wealth so that you end up poor. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: do not withhold charity. [Yaman ibn Ribab] said: "and do not squander wastefully." Mujahid and Ata al-Awfi said: "and do not leave the idols in the field and the cattle."

Al-Zuhri said: [they fell into] sin. Mujahid said: if Abu Qubays were gold belonging to a man, and he spent it in obedience to God, he would not be extravagant; but if he spent a dirham or a mudd in disobedience to God, he would be extravagant. In this sense, it was said to Hatim al-Ta'i: "There is no good in extravagance," and he said: "There is no extravagance in good."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: extravagance is not giving what is due. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: extravagance is what one cannot restore to rightness, and corruption is what one can restore to rightness.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: extravagance is squandering and excess, while "sarf" is heedlessness and ignorance. A poet said:

"Give to Hunayda, whom eight [camels] drive along, there is no excess or extravagance in their giving."
[The verse is by Jarir, as in al-Kanz al-Lughawi of Ibn al-Sikkit al-Ahwazi, p. 116.]

Iyas ibn Mu'awiya said: whatever exceeds God's command is extravagance. Ibn Wahb narrated from Ibn Zayd who said: the address is to the poor: "do not take more than your right."

﴿And of the cattle﴾, meaning He produced from the cattle ﴿carriers﴾ (hamulatan), meaning everything that is loaded upon and ridden, such as large camels, cows, horses, mules and donkeys. They were named so because they carry their loads. Antara said:

"Nothing called me except the carriers of its people, in the middle of the dwellings, sweeping the dust of the khumkhum (plant)."
[Lisan al-Arab: 12/191.]

And hamulah means loads.

The lexicographers said: the pattern fa'ula, with a fatḥa on the fa', when it means the doer, applies equally to the masculine and feminine, such as: "rajul farruqa" and "imra'a farruqa" (a coward/fearful man and woman); "rajul ṣarura" and "imra'a ṣarura" when they have not performed the pilgrimage. When it means the object, the masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ha', like khalawiyya and zakawiyya. ﴿And as the carpets (farshan)﴾: the farsh are those that are eaten and milked, and not carried upon, such as sheep, young camels and young calves. They were called farsh (carpets/low-lying) because of the delicacy of their bodies and their closeness to the ground. Farsh is the level earth; the root of farsh is lightness and delicacy, and from it comes firasha al-'aql (the lightness of intellect) and firash al-'izam (the thin layer of bone). Farsh is also a plant clinging to the ground which camels eat. The rajiz said:

"Like the broken tooth chewing the farsh."
[Lisan al-Arab: 6/317.]

Farsh also means young offspring of livestock. The rajiz said:

"He bequeathed to me carriers and young ones, I milk them every day, milk by milk."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/112; mashsh al-naqa means to milk the she-camel.]

﴿Eat of what God has provided you, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan; indeed he is to you a clear enemy﴾, [which] forbade the crops and the cattle. Then He explained the carriers and the carpets, saying: ﴿eight pairs﴾, put in the accusative as a substitute for "carriers" [by the obligation], meaning: [one of] the cattle: eight pairs, that is, eight kinds: ﴿of the sheep, two﴾, so the male is a pair and the female is a pair. The word ḍa'n (sheep) and na'aj are its plural; its singular is ḍa'in, its feminine is ḍa'ina, and its plural is ḍawa'in.

al-Hasan and Talha ibn Musarrif read "al-ḍa'n" with a fatḥa on the hamza; the others read it with a sukun on the hamza. The Tamim [pronounce it] with a hamza, and the rest without a hamza. ﴿And of the goats, two﴾. The ma'z is the mu'za (goat); it has no singular from its own form. As for the mā'iz, its plural is ma'iza, and the plural of mā'iza is mawā'iz. The people of Medina and Kufa read ﴿min al-ma'z﴾ with a sukun on the 'ayn, and the others with a fatḥa. In the codex of Ubayy: "min al-ma'za." Aban ibn Uthman read: "min al-ḍa'n ithnan, wa-min al-ma'z ithnayn." Say, O Muhammad: ﴿Is it the two males that He has forbidden, or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain?﴾ — the male of the sheep, or the female? Or the female of the goat or its female? [The accusative] is in His saying ﴿the two males, has He forbidden, or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain﴾. ﴿Tell me with knowledge, if you are truthful.﴾ ﴿And of the camels, two, and of the cattle, two.﴾ ﴿Say: Is it the two males He has forbidden, or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain?﴾

This was because they used to say: "These are cattle and a forbidden tilth," and they said: "What is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives." So they forbade the baḥīra, the sā'iba, the waṣīla and the ḥām.

When Islam arose and the rulings were established, they argued with the Prophet (ﷺ). Their spokesman that day was Malik ibn Awf and Abu al-Nadr [al-Nasri], and he said: "O Muhammad, do we see that you forbid what our fathers used to do?"

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "You have forbidden kinds of livestock upon [...] [unclear text]. God created these eight pairs for eating and benefit. So from where have you forbidden the males of these livestock to your women and not to your men? If you claim that its prohibition is because of the males, you must forbid every male, since males have a share in them; and if you claim that its prohibition is from the side of the female, you must forbid every female, since females have a share in them; and if you claim that its prohibition is due to the male and female being together in it, and what the womb contains, you must forbid the male and the female, the living and the dead, since there is no offspring except from a male and female, and the womb contains only a male and female. Why do you forbid some and permit some?" Then he (they) fell silent.

When he was overcome by the proof, he resorted to slandering God, saying: "Thus God has commanded us."

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or were you witnesses when God enjoined this upon you?﴾ [present].

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God, to lead people astray without knowledge? Indeed God does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

﴿Except that it be carrion (maytatan) or flowing blood (damman masfūḥan)﴾ — poured forth (muhraqan), flowing. ʿImran ibn Jarir said: I asked Abu Mijlaz about meat smeared with blood, and about a cooking pot on which a reddish trace of blood appears. He said: There is no harm in it; Allah, glorified is He, only forbade flowing blood.

Ibrahim said: There is no harm in blood in veins or marrow, except flowing blood, which one deliberately allows. ʿIkrima said:

Had it not been for this verse, Muslims would have followed the veins as much as the Jews followed them [[See the tafsir of al-Qurtubi: 7/124.]].

﴿Or the flesh of swine, for it is impure (rijs), abominable; or an act of wickedness (fisqan), a sin, over which a name other than Allah has been invoked (uhilla li-ghayr Allah bihi). But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿And to those who were Jews (alladhina hadu) — that is, the Jews — We forbade every animal with a claw (kulla dhi zufr), which is what does not have split hooves among animals and birds, such as camels, ostriches, geese, and ducks.﴾

Ibn Zayd said: It refers only to camels. Al-Qutaybi said: It is every bird with talons and every solid-hoofed animal, and he attributed this to some exegetes. It was also said: the hoof was called a claw (zufr) by metaphor, and he recited the verse of Tarafa:

"The youths did not sleep until they saw him on the young she-camel, driving her with shank and hoof."
[[The line is by Jubayha al-Asadi, as in Lisan al-Arab: 4/206.]]

Thus the hoof is placed in the position of the foot.

al-Hasan recited kulla dhi ẓifrin with a kasra on the ẓāʾ and a sukun on the fāʾ. [Abu Simak] recited ẓifirin with a kasra on both the ẓāʾ and the fāʾ, and this is a dialectal form.

﴿And from cattle and sheep We forbade them their fats, except what their backs carry or the entrails (al-hawaya), or what is mixed with bone.﴾ This means the [fat of the kidneys?] and the fat of the two kidneys, except what is carried on their backs, that is, what clings to the back and flank, except what is inside their bellies. Al-hawaya refers to goats. Or what is mixed with bone, such as the fat of the rump. That prohibition We recompensed them for their rebellion (bighyihim), for their wrongdoing, as a punishment for them for killing the prophets, barring others from the path of Allah, taking usury, and devouring people's wealth falsely. ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ in Our reports about these Jews and about what We forbade them of meats and fats.

﴿Those who associated partners will say: [Since the proof has been established against them], and they have understood and become certain that what they were upon is false: "Had Allah willed, we would not have associated [others with Him], nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything"﴾ — such as the bahira and the sa'iba and other things. For He is capable of preventing us from this, so that we would not do it; but He was pleased with what we are upon, worshipping idols and forbidding the tilled field and cattle, and He willed it of us and commanded us with it, and did not prevent us from it. Then Allah, exalted is He, said, rejecting them and refuting them: ﴿Thus did those before them deny﴾. Had it been as they claim, Allah, exalted above what those who denied them said, would have said: "Thus did those before them" (kadhdhaba, with a light dhāl), and He would have attributed to them lying, not denial.

al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: [When they uttered this statement,] it was in glorification and majesty of Allah, exalted and glorified, and a description of Him on their part when they were rebuked for it, because Allah says: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have associated﴾ and He says: ﴿They would not have believed unless Allah willed﴾ and ﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾. The believers say this too, but they said it as denial, conjecture, and substitution without knowledge of Allah and of what [they say]. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And they say: Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [[Surah al-Zukhruf: 20.]]. Allah said: ﴿They have no knowledge of that; they only guess﴾ — by their saying this, without knowledge, which He explained with a sign, for the believers, and His saying, and knowledge from them of Allah, mighty and majestic. Then He said: ﴿Do you have any knowledge?﴾ — any share or proof for what they say without knowledge and certainty. ﴿You are only guessing﴾ — lying.

﴿Say: To Allah belongs the conclusive proof (al-hujjat al-baligha), the complete and sufficient over His creation. So had He willed, He would have guided you all.﴾ ﴿Say: Bring forward your witnesses who testify that Allah forbade this﴾ — that is, bring them and produce them. They said: "We testify." Allah said: ﴿If they testify, do not testify with them﴾ up to His saying ﴿they equate﴾ — they associate others with Him.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 6, verse 151–155:

Then He said: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you"﴾ — (Say, O Muhammad, "Come, I will recite" — I will read — "what your Lord has forbidden you" — "truly," certainly, "as I was revealed to by my Lord, and He commanded me with it," not conjecture nor denial, "as they claim." ﴿That you associate nothing with Him﴾.

They differed regarding the grammatical position (maḥall) of "an" (that). Some said: its position is in the accusative (naṣb). Then they differed regarding the manner of its being in the accusative. It was said: its meaning is "He forbade that you associate," and the "lā" is superfluous (ṣila), like their saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ (mā manaʿaka allā tasjuda).

It was said: "that you do not associate" follows from "I have been commanded that..." It was said: "Revealed that you not associate." It was said: [mā] is a substitute (badal) [for] "what He forbade." It was said: the speech ends at His saying "your Lord has forbidden you," and then He said: "It is incumbent upon you that you do not associate," in opposition to disbelief. Some said:

The position of [min] means: "namely that you do not associate openly with your disbelief." As for what follows it, it is permissible that it be in the accusative position, conjoined (ʿaṭf) to His saying "that you associate not." And "an" [ ... ] [[an unreadable word.]] because it is permissible that it be jazm (apocopated) according to the stronger view, like His saying: ﴿Say: "I have been commanded that I be the first of those who submit"﴾.

﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ — a conjunction of a prohibition upon a statement (ʿaṭf bil-nahy ʿalā al-khabar). The poet said:

Perform the pilgrimage and bequeath Sulaymā to none but a slave... that she sees no one and speaks to no one

And her drink never ceases to be cooled.

[[Tafsir al-Tabari 8: 108.]]

﴿And to parents, kindness; and do not kill your children out of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾ — and do not bury your daughters alive out of fear of want; for I provide for you and for them. Al-imlāq is poverty and the exhaustion of provisions.

﴿And do not approach the abominations, what is apparent of them﴾ — meaning openly, ﴿and what is hidden﴾ — meaning secretly. The exegetes said:

In the Jahiliyyah they regarded fornication as abhorrent in public, but saw no harm in it in private, so God forbade fornication both openly and secretly. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "what is apparent" is wine, "and what is hidden" ... ﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾ — meaning that which He has forbidden, namely a believing soul or one under covenant (muʿāhad), ﴿except by right﴾ — meaning by what He has permitted before it, namely apostasy, retaliation (qiṣāṣ), and stoning.

Maṭar al-Warrāq narrated from Nāfiʿ ibn ʿUmar, from ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, that he looked down upon his companions and said:

"On what account do they kill me? For I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: a man who commits adultery after his marriage, so for him is stoning; or one who kills intentionally, so for him is retaliation; or one who apostatizes after his Islam, so for him is execution. By Allah, I have not committed adultery in the Jahiliyyah nor in Islam, nor have I killed anyone so as to be retaliated against, nor have I apostatized since I embraced Islam. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger.'" [160] [[al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā: 3/67.]]

﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand﴾ — that is, the Prophet I mentioned. ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ — meaning with what is good for it and its growth. Mujāhid said: it is trading with it. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: wealth that is sought for him, and he does not take from its profit anything.

Ibn Zayd said: and that he eats in accordance with what is customary if he is poor, and if he is rich he does not eat. al-Shaʿbī said: whoever mixes with the orphan's property until it is separated from him, let him mix with it; and whoever mixes with it so as to eat from it, let him leave it until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu).

Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar said: it is the attainment of puberty. al-Shaʿbī said: the ashudd is the age of reason, when good deeds are written for him and bad deeds against him. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: until he understands and his strength is gathered.

al-Kalbī said: al-ashudd is between eighteen and thirty years. al-Suddī said: it is thirty years, then after it he continues until they reach marriage.

Al-ashudd is the plural of shadd, like qadd and aqadd, and it is the full strength of a youth, his vigour and his age; and from it is "shadd al-nahār," which is its height. It is said: "I came to him at shadd al-nahār" and "madd al-nahār." Al-Faḍl ibn Muḥammad said concerning the shadd in the verse of ʿAntarah:

[ʿahdī bihi] shadd al-nahār as though ... his chest was dyed and his head with ʿaẓlam [[Lisān al-ʿArab: 3/235.]]

Another said:

Around him shadd al-nahār is a she-camel... long, clean-handed, sturdy [[Lisān al-ʿArab: 10/154.]]

And reaching the ashudd is not something that leaves the nearness to his property except in the best manner, and the speech is complete.

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ [forever] ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾, then give him his property if he is sound of judgment. ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice﴾ — with fairness, ﴿We do not charge any soul except according to its capacity﴾ — that is, its ability in giving full measure and weight. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿānī) said: its meaning is: except what it can bear, and what is lawful for it, and it does not go beyond it nor is it constricted by it. That is because God, among His servants, has that many of them constrict their souls from being pleased to give to another what is not obligatory upon them; so He commanded the giver to give the right to its owner, and charged him with the excess, because of the constriction of his soul over it; and He commanded the one who is owed to take his right, and did not charge him with being content with less than it, because of the constriction of his soul in the deficiency. So He did not charge either of the two souls except with what carries no hardship and is not constricting for them.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: "You, O non-Arabs, have been entrusted with two matters by which those before you perished: the measure and the scale." ﴿And when you speak, be just﴾ — that is, be truthful in judgment and testimony, ﴿even if it be a near relative﴾ — the subject is omitted, meaning even if the one judged or testified against is a relative. ﴿And fulfill the covenant of God; that He has enjoined upon you, that you may remember﴾ — that is, that you may take heed.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: these verses are clear (muḥkamāt); nothing has abrogated them in all the scriptures, and they are forbidden to all of the children of Adam, and they are the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitāb). Whoever acts upon them enters Paradise, and whoever abandons them enters Hellfire.

Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said: "By Him in whose hand is Kaʿb's soul, this is indeed the first thing in the Torah: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate... Say: 'Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you,' the verses."

al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said to his companions: "Shall I not recite to you a scroll upon which is the seal of Muhammad ﷺ, unbroken?" and he recited this verse: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite"﴾, and that this — meaning He enjoined you with it in these two verses: ﴿This is My path, straight﴾ — My way and My religion, upright, sound, ﴿so follow it; and do not follow the [other] ways﴾ — meaning the various paths other than it, such as Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and the rest of innovations and misguidance, ﴿lest they separate you from His way﴾ — away from His path, and the religion of the Prophet that He has approved, and with which He enjoined. ﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may be righteous.﴾

﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾ — meaning: then say, O Muhammad, to them: We gave Moses the Book, because Moses was given the Book before Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them both. It was said: "thumma" here means "wa" (and), since both are conjunctive particles. The poet said:

Say to him who ruled, then his father ruled, then his grandfather had ruled before that...

[[The verse is by Abū Nuwās in praise of al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, as in al-Raḍī's commentary on al-Kāfiyah: 4/390.]]

﴿Completely﴾ is in the accusative on the basis of a circumstantial/discontinuous construction (qaṭʿ), and it was said: by way of explanation. ﴿Upon the one who did good﴾. Some said: its meaning is "completely for the good-doers," and "alladhī" carries the sense of "man," its intended meaning being "upon those who did good"; its wording is singular but its meaning is plural, just as you say: "I bequeath my wealth to the one who fought and performed the pilgrimage," meaning the fighters and the pilgrims.

The poet said:

They raised glory for me and grew old, and he became mature...

He means: "and they became mature."

What indicates this is the reading of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd: "upon those who did good."

Abū ʿUbayd said: its meaning is "upon every one who did good," and the meaning of this view is: we completed Moses' [request] with this Book, for the good-doers, meaning we manifested his excellence over them; and the good-doers are the prophets and the believers. It was said: its meaning is: ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾ completing for the good-doers, meaning a completion from us for the prophets and the believing books; ("ʿalā") is in the sense of ("lām"), as you say: "God completed it upon him, and completed it for him." The poet said:

She pastured for months and was left to them... so the one in them flew and sought refuge

He means: "and was left for her."

It was said: "alladhī" means "mā," meaning: We gave Moses the Book, completely upon what Moses excelled in of knowledge and wisdom, that is, in addition to that.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Buraydah said: its meaning is completion from me upon my favour and my kindness to Moses. Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is completion upon God's kindness to His prophets and His bounties upon them. al-Ḥasan said: among them is the good-doer and among them is the wrongdoer, so the Book was sent down as a completion upon the good-doers. Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar read: "ʿalā alladhī aḥsanu" with a raised vowel, meaning "upon him who did good."

﴿And as a detailed explanation of everything needed of the laws of the religion, and as guidance and mercy; that perhaps they would believe in the meeting with their Lord.﴾ This — meaning: and this Qur'an, ﴿is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it﴾ — act upon what is in it, ﴿and fear God and obey, that perhaps you may be shown mercy﴾ — so that you are not punished.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: these verses are clear (muḥkamāt); nothing has abrogated them in all the scriptures, and they are forbidden to all of the children of Adam, and they are the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitāb). Whoever acts upon them enters Paradise, and whoever abandons them enters Hellfire.

Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said: "By Him in whose hand is Kaʿb's soul, this is indeed the first thing in the Torah: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate... Say: 'Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you,' the verses."

Say to him who ruled, then his father ruled, then his grandfather had ruled before that...

He means: "and they became mature."

He means: "and was left for her."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 6, verses 156–165 (part 2 of 2):

The common reciters read the ya' with a fatha, so that two consonants are not brought together (lā yajtami'a sākinān). Ibn Abi Ishaq and Isa read "wa-mahyyā" with the second ya' doubled and without an alif, and this is the dialect of the upper Mudar, who say "qafyy" and "casyy." Al-Sulami read "nusuki" with a sukun on the sin, while the rest read it with two dammas.

﴿Say: Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds. He has no partner. And this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims.﴾

Qatadah said: "The first of the Muslims of this community." al-Kalbi said: "The first to obey Allah among the people of his time."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Imran ibn [Husayn], who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Fatimah, stand up and witness your sacrifice, for with the first drop of its blood every sin you have committed will be forgiven. Then say: ﴿Indeed my prayer and my sacrifice…﴾ up to His words ﴿…the first of the Muslims.﴾"

Imran said: "O Messenger of Allah, is this verse specific to the People of your House, or is it for the Muslims in general?"

He said: "Rather, it is for the Muslims in general."

(Kanz al-'Ummal: 5/102, hadith 12236.)

﴿Say: Shall I seek a lord other than Allah, while He is the Lord of everything?﴾ — i.e., shall I seek a master besides Allah?

﴿And every soul earns only against itself﴾ — i.e., it is not taken to account for anything except the sins it has committed and perpetrated, and not for the sins of others.

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ — meaning: no soul shall bear the sins of another soul upon itself, nor shall a sinful soul be made to sin for another's sin; rather, every soul is seized for its own offence and punished for its own sin.

﴿Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ.﴾

﴿And it is He who made you successors (khala'if) on the earth﴾ — meaning: the people of the past generations and the bygone nations, and He made you inheritors of the earth after them, then made you successors among them in what they left behind, cultivating it after them. Khala'if is the plural of khalifah, like wasif (servant) whose plural is wasifah. Whoever comes after one who has passed is a khalifah. It is said: "Fulan succeeded (khalafa) Fulan in his house, succeeding him in succession (khilafah), so he is a khalifah," as al-Shammakh said:

"Misfortunes strike them and miss me, and I succeed in one abode after another." (Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/150; Lisan al-'Arab: 8/102.)

﴿And He raised some of you above others in degrees﴾ — meaning: and He varied your conditions, making some of you superior to others in creation, provision, strength, expansiveness, knowledge, virtue, livelihood and the hereafter.

﴿That He may test you in what He has given you﴾ — meaning: wealth and poverty, the noble and the lowly, the free and the slave.

﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾ — meaning: what is coming is near. It was also said: it refers to destruction in this world.

al-Kalbi said: "When He punishes, His punishment is swift." Ata said: "Swift in punishing His enemies."

﴿And indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ — to His friends.
